{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-02",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["Storefront client", "Public GraphQL endpoint", "GraphQL resolvers", "Product service", "Review service", "Customer profile service"],
    "dataStores": ["Product catalog", "Reviews store", "Customer profile store"],
    "externalServices": [],
    "trustBoundaries": ["Internet to public GraphQL endpoint", "GraphQL resolvers to backend data stores"],
    "dataClasses": ["pii"],
    "exposure": "public",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Anyone on the internet can query other customers' profile data",
      "scenario": "The endpoint is public and the design does not describe any authentication or per-object authorization on the customer profile fields. An attacker sends a query for customerProfile(id: ...) or walks ids/emails through the products->reviews->customer path and reads names, emails, addresses and order history for arbitrary customers at scale, then sells or phishes the list.",
      "component": "Public GraphQL endpoint - customer profile resolvers",
      "likelihood": 5,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The storefront uses a public GraphQL endpoint. Clients can request nested queries of products, reviews and customer profiles." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V8.1.1", "V8.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-639", "CWE-306"],
      "plainLanguage": "Because the API is open to everyone, someone could ask it for other shoppers' personal details just by changing an id in the request.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Authorize every customer profile field on the server",
        "given": "an unauthenticated or non-owner caller on the public GraphQL endpoint",
        "when": "the query selects customerProfile fields directly or through products or reviews",
        "then": "the resolver checks the session identity against the profile owner and returns an authorization error instead of the data"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Nested queries leak personal data through product and review paths",
      "scenario": "Even if the top-level profile query is protected, nesting lets an attacker reach PII sideways: product -> reviews -> author -> customerProfile -> email/address. Authorization applied only at the entry point is bypassed because each resolver trusts its parent. An attacker enumerates the public catalog and harvests reviewer identities and contact data.",
      "component": "GraphQL resolvers - nested review and author edges",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Clients can request nested queries of products, reviews and customer profiles." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V8.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-285", "CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "A query can start at a public product, hop to its reviews, then to the reviewer's profile, and pull out private details the API meant to hide.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Enforce field-level authorization on every edge, not just root queries",
        "given": "a query that reaches customer data through a nested product or review edge",
        "when": "the resolver for that field executes",
        "then": "the same authorization check runs as for the root profile query and unauthorized fields resolve to null with an error"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "DenialOfService",
      "title": "Deeply nested or recursive query exhausts the API and databases",
      "scenario": "An unauthenticated attacker posts a single query that recurses product -> reviews -> author -> reviews -> product many levels deep, or uses many aliases in one request. With no depth, complexity or cost limit described, one request fans out to millions of backend reads and takes the storefront API offline during a sales event.",
      "component": "Public GraphQL endpoint - query execution",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Clients can request nested queries of products, reviews and customer profiles." },
        { "quote": "The storefront uses a public GraphQL endpoint." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-770", "CWE-674"],
      "plainLanguage": "One cleverly written request can ask for so much nested data that it knocks the shop's API over.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Limit query depth and cost",
        "given": "any request to the public GraphQL endpoint",
        "when": "the query exceeds the configured maximum depth, alias count or computed complexity cost",
        "then": "the request is rejected before execution with a 4xx error and the limit is enforced for unauthenticated callers too"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Production introspection hands attackers the full attack map",
      "scenario": "With introspection on in production, anyone can download the complete schema, including internal, admin or not-yet-launched fields and mutations that were never meant for the storefront. An attacker uses it to find unprotected customer or pricing fields in minutes instead of guessing, and to script exploitation of them.",
      "component": "Public GraphQL endpoint - introspection",
      "likelihood": 5,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Introspection is enabled in production." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V13.4.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "The API publishes a complete list of everything it can do, so an attacker does not have to guess what to try.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Disable introspection on the public production endpoint",
        "given": "a caller on the production GraphQL endpoint",
        "when": "an __schema or __type introspection query is sent",
        "then": "the request is rejected, and the schema is published to developers through a separate non-production or authenticated channel"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "Hidden mutations reachable because the endpoint is shared and public",
      "scenario": "A single public endpoint serving products, reviews and profiles typically also exposes mutations such as updateProfile or deleteReview. An attacker who discovered them via introspection calls them with another customer's id. Without per-mutation authorization, they change someone else's email or address and then take over the account through password reset.",
      "component": "Public GraphQL endpoint - mutations",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The storefront uses a public GraphQL endpoint." },
        { "quote": "Introspection is enabled in production." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V8.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-862"],
      "plainLanguage": "If write operations sit on the same open endpoint, someone could edit another shopper's account details and then take it over.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Separate and authorize write operations",
        "given": "a mutation on the public GraphQL endpoint",
        "when": "the caller is unauthenticated or is not the owner of the target record",
        "then": "the mutation is refused and no data is written"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Query batching and aliasing defeat rate limits for enumeration and credential attacks",
      "scenario": "GraphQL lets an attacker pack hundreds of aliased operations into one HTTP request. Per-request rate limiting on the public endpoint then counts that as a single call, so the attacker enumerates customer ids, coupon codes or login/reset operations thousands of times per minute from one IP without tripping throttles.",
      "component": "Public GraphQL endpoint - batching and aliases",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The storefront uses a public GraphQL endpoint. Clients can request nested queries of products, reviews and customer profiles." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-307", "CWE-799"],
      "plainLanguage": "Many attempts can be hidden inside one request, so normal 'too many requests' protection never kicks in.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Rate limit per resolved operation, not per HTTP request",
        "given": "a request containing batched operations or repeated aliased fields",
        "when": "rate limits are evaluated",
        "then": "each resolved operation counts toward the limit and over-limit requests are rejected, with batching disabled unless it is required"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Verbose GraphQL errors reveal internal structure and data",
      "scenario": "Default GraphQL servers return resolver stack traces, SQL fragments, internal field and type names, and 'did you mean' field suggestions. On a public endpoint these let an attacker reconstruct the schema even after introspection is disabled, and learn database and service internals to target further attacks.",
      "component": "Public GraphQL endpoint - error handling",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The storefront uses a public GraphQL endpoint." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V13.4.2"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-209"],
      "plainLanguage": "Error messages can tell an attacker how the system is built inside, including hints about field names it should not reveal.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Return sanitized errors to public callers",
        "given": "a query that causes a resolver or validation error",
        "when": "the response is built for a public caller",
        "then": "only a generic message and error code are returned, with stack traces, query suggestions and backend details kept in server-side logs only"
      }
    }
  ]
}
